about: The century before day one (owner, Nov 17, 2026, CTO line 6935086070 on #9747: "History is pure simulation from 1925, a year at a step, during the loading screen ... Day one is whatever that history produced ... Real data only sets how strongly things move one another."). Read by src/core2/century.ts. Every number is tagged SOURCED, ESTIMATED or TUNABLE and carries its role.

centuryFirstYear.source: The owner's ruling, Nov 17, 2026 (CTO line 6935086070 on #9747): "Oh, 1925? Okay. I didn't know if I could be that ambitious, but sure. Absolutely."

centuryStateLeanSpread.source: How far apart the states stand when the century opens, as a spread for each state's one starting shift (electorate-century.ts centuryShift, any size between -1 and 1 of the spread equally likely, so its mean size is half of it). Sized so the mean distance of a state from the nation is the 2024 map's: across the 51 presidential electorates the mean absolute gap of a state's Republican two-party share from the vote-weighted national share is 0.0951 (data/source/electoral-calibration-2024/corpus.json, presidentialByState; 0.0951 / 0.5 = 0.19). The spread calibrates how much states differ; which state stands where is the world's.

centuryNationalLeanSpread.source: The spread of the whole country's one starting shift on the lean order in 1925, on top of each state's own. Checked against the 2024 national Republican two-party share's distance from even (0.507, the same corpus): up to a few points either way, any size equally likely (centuryShift).

centuryLeanCarryShare.source: How much of a state's last presidential result, cleared of what was personal to the two candidates (an incumbent's and an officeholder's edge), stays in where the state stands for the next one. A strength, not a target: a state's lean is its own last result carried, never pulled toward a figure. Checked against the persistence of state two-party shares from one presidential election to the next (state results correlate strongly election to election); to be sourced from state returns (research item history-lean-carry-strength) and shared with the voting engine's lean carry (World B, audit item 1).

centuryVoters.source: How many voters, evenly spaced along the lean order at the typical readiness of a presidential year, stand for a place when the century counts it (stopgap SG-HIST-century-voters). The count's rule is the engine's own (electorate.ts countPlaces, each record dividing over its own stretch of the order); the number only sets how finely turnout is weighed along it. Measured against 400 (the town's coarse sample size, coarseSampleVoters) at seeds a1, b2 and c3 on Nov 17, 2026, with the record-stretch count: the century's 25 presidential winners matched at 100, 40 and 20 voters in a1 and b2, and at 100 and 40 in c3 (20 moved 10); day one's 541 seats in Congress matched at 100, and differed in 1, 0 and 0 at 40, and 2, 2 and 10 at 20. A century cost 4.7 to 5.3 s at 400, 1.5 to 1.6 s at 100 and 0.76 to 1.0 s at 40.

centuryHiddenVoters.source: How many voters, evenly spaced along the lean order, stand for a district of another state's legislature, counted as results until someone opens its member (the played town's state and Congress keep centuryVoters). The count's rule is the engine's own; the number only sets how finely turnout is weighed. Measured against 40 on Nov 17, 2026 (seeds named in the pull request): at seeds leg-a, leg-b and leg-c (town states Texas, Texas, Ohio), 20 voters ended the century with 33, 32 and 44 of 7,419 legislative seats on the other side than 40 did (under half a percent), no two races sharing a share at either, and the legislatures' pass took 3.0 to 3.3 s against 4.7 to 5.5 s. #9883's golden-path spec M2-07 had timed out by half a second at 40.

presidentialTermYears.source: U.S. Const. art. II, § 1: the President holds office during a term of four years.

inaugurationMovedYear.source: U.S. Const. amend. XX, § 1 (ratified 1933): terms begin at noon on January 20; the first term to begin then was the one beginning in 1937. Before it, on March 4.

twoTermBarFirstElection.source: U.S. Const. amend. XXII, § 1 (ratified February 27, 1951): no person shall be elected to the office of the President more than twice. The first election it governed was 1952.

centuryDistrictLeanSpread.source: How far a House district stands from its state when the century opens, as the spread of each district's one starting shift (electorate-century.ts centuryShift, any size between -1 and 1 of the spread equally likely, so its mean size is half of it). Sized so the mean distance is the 2024 map's: across 397 contested House districts the mean absolute gap of a district's Republican two-party share from its state's presidential share is 0.1038 (data/source/electoral-calibration-2024/corpus.json, house and presidentialByState; 0.1038 / 0.5 = 0.208). Calibration of how much districts differ; which district stands where is the world's. State legislative districts take the same spread until their own is sourced (the 2024 state legislative returns by district).

senateClassOneYear.source: U.S. Const. art. I, sec. 3: senators are divided into three classes, one elected every second year for six-year terms. Class 1 was elected in 2024, class 2 in 2026's cycle (2020), class 3 in 2028's (2022); data/research/offices/senate-classes-2026.json names each state's classes.

centuryDistrictSizeSpread.source: How far a district's eligible voters stand from its chamber's typical (the state's eligible over its districts), as a share either side: each district's multiple is 1 + spread x (2u - 1) for its own seeded unit. Districts hold near equal people by law (Wesberry v. Sanders, 376 U.S. 1 (1964); Reynolds v. Sims, 377 U.S. 533 (1964); a state legislative plan under 10 percent total deviation is presumed valid, Brown v. Thomson, 462 U.S. 835 (1983)), but not equal citizens of voting age, who differ with age and citizenship by district. Generation of who lives where, never an outcome. Not yet sourced: the spread of citizen voting-age population across districts in the Census Bureau's CVAP special tabulation (research item history-district-size-spread).

centuryCampaignMeansLogSpread.source: How far a century candidate's campaign means stand from the typical race's, on a natural-log scale: each candidate's multiple is exp(spread x (2u - 1)) for their own seeded unit, so between about a third and about three times the typical. Generation of who exists (their donors, own money and party backing), read by the one race rule's spending reason (spendingSharePerLogUnit, 0.015 a log unit), so it moves a candidate by at most about 1.5 points. Not yet sourced: the spread of House and statewide candidates' receipts around their race's typical in FEC and state filings (research item history-campaign-means-spread).
